title: OGEC Staff Advisory Opinion 15S-004: Conflicts of interest for council members deciding regulations on short-term vacation rentals.

Dear Mr. Kearns:

This is in response to your correspondence received by the Oregon Government Ethics
Commission on September 30, 2015, regarding conflict of interest implications for two
city council members for the City of Hood River when considering matters involving short-
term vacation rentals that are likely to come before City Council.

OREGON GOVERNMENT ETHICS COMMISSION STAFF ADVISORY OPINION NO.
15$-004:

STATED FACTS: On August 17, 2015, City Council for the City of Hood River reviewed
and adopted the results of an updated Housing Needs Analysis. Results of the Housing
Needs Analysis showed that the City is currently experiencing a deficiency in affordable
housing, in part, due to a large proportion of the City’s available housing being used for
short-term vacation rentals (“STRs”). In addressing the housing deficiency, City Council
adopted three recommended guidelines for the Planning Commission to use when
undertaking the process, one of which is specifically directed toward “Regulating and
managing secondary and short-term rental housing.” Pursuant to this guideline, the City’s
strategy is to adopt a regulatory scheme in a three-step process that is likely to lead City
Council to decide whether to adopt STR regulations in the following forms:

e “Registration System”. Require STRs to obtain a license and pay an annual
renewal fee in order to operate. The type of licensing fee currently under
consideration would be a flat fee ($200 - $300) per unit or per property for initial
licensing, as well as for annual renewal. Each license would be limited for use only
by the property or unit located at the address for which the license is issued; a
license issued for one STR would not be transferrable, by owner or otherwise, to
any other property. No STR would be permitted to operate without a license.

e “Operational Regulations”. Develop a set of STR-specific business regulations that
work to minimize nuisances and maintain public health and safety. Examples of
contemplated regulations include the following: occupancy load limits (according
to number of bedrooms, bathrooms, or square feet); trash collection standards;
limitations or requirements for parking; requiring a local contact (as well as
determining what is “local”); and requirements for homeowners insurance and
safety inspections.

e¢ “Limit on Numbers”. Cap the number of STRs citywide. The City might accomplish
this by limiting the total number or maximum density of STRs citywide or based on
land use application or housing type. City Council has directed staff not to develop
the plan based on neighborhood or street boundaries. Caps could cause
discontinuation of some currently existing STRs.

The City must also consider how to define “short term vacation rentals”, as well as
whether to add sub-categories of STRs that may be separately delineated under
proposed regulations: “hosted” (where the owner or landlord occupies the property)
versus “non-hosted”: or differentiating between local, in-state, and out-of-state ownership
of STR properties.

There are predicted to be several hundred STRs operating in the City of Hood River (City
population approximately 7500), and two members of City Council who have been
involved in the business could be affected by any STR regulations. One of these city
councilors owns a home in Hood River, which he occasionally offers for rent as an STR
in the summer. During times when his Hood River home is rented out, he stays at a
residence in Portland. The other city councilor offers a room in her home as a short-term
rental, but she remains in her home with the STR-occupant while the room is rented.

City Council is scheduled to discuss some of the operative definitions regarding STRs at
its November 9'" meeting.

QUESTION 1: Whether conflicts of interest may arise for members of city council if
matters involving regulation of short-term vacation rentals come before City Council.

ANSWER 1: Yes. City councilors can be met with conflicts of interest when their official
actions, decisions, or recommendations would or could result in a private financial benefit
to themselves.

Oregon Government Ethics law defines two conflicts of interest, “actual” [ORS
244.020(1)] and “potential” [ORS 244.020(12)]. The difference between an actual conflict
of interest and a potential conflict of interest is determined by the words “would” and
“could”. An actual conflict of interest occurs when a public official participates in an official
action that would have a direct and specific financial impact on that public official, a

Daniel Kearns

Commission Staff Advisory Opinion 15S-004
November 9, 2015

Page 3

relative, or any business with which any is associated. A potential conflict arises when a
public official takes action that could possibly have a financial impact on the public official,
a relative, or any business with which any is associated. (Also, please note that although
conflicts of interest are analyzed directly here, if any exception under ORS 244,020(12)
(as discussed in Question 2) applies, it is as if no conflict exists; determining the type of
conflict and method of handling under ORS 244.120 would be unnecessary.)

Based on the facts provided, any of the proposed STR definitions or regulations at least
could financially impact the two city councilors who currently maintain such properties,
but it is also worth briefly noting that the same can also be said for any who may be
considering rental of their own properties as STRs in the future. Thus, for any city
councilors who might think of themselves as potential future STR-owners, potential
conflicts should always be announced before participating in any discussion or decision
as to proposed definitions or regulations [ORS 244.120(2)]. As for the two city councilors
who actually have a record of maintaining STR properties, both actual and potential
conflicts may arise. However, it is unclear whether actual conflicts would arise—i.e.,
whether personal financial impact is certain and specific—in all circumstances. The
answers appear to largely depend on the specific regulation or ordinance contemplated,
as well as the stage of the implementation process. Public officials are individually
responsible for determining when it is necessary to declare a conflict of interest.

Acting as a city councilor to work toward forming any kind of regulation in its preliminary
stages (such as engaging in discussion, debate, or recommendation of any contemplated
regulation(s)) would, at most, constitute a potential conflict of interest for any city councilor
who may be financially impacted by the regulation. This is because in these early stages
of the process, it is impossible to know how a regulation will take final form, or whether it
will ever even make it to the Council for a vote. Thus, any resulting financial impact is
inherently uncertain. On the other hand, once a contemplated regulation is put to the
Council for final decision-making or approval, it may, at that point, rise to an actual conflict
where a certain and specific financial impact to the city councilor(s) can be identified. A
more specific analysis as to actual conflicts in final decision-making follows:

Operative Definitions. It appears that potential conflicts of interest will exist when, prior
to determining any specific regulations, City Council decides what sorts of properties
should be considered STRs and what, if any, additional property categories should exist.
No actual conflict would appear to arise, because no certain or specific financial benefit
can be identified absent any regulations. However, as regulations that might financially
affect defined properties are currently under contemplation, it appears highly likely that
the city councilors could be financially affected by attendant regulation in the near future
(or by exclusion from any approved definition(s)). Thus, potential conflicts must be
publicly announced prior to participating in discussion or approval [see ORS 244,120(2)].

Daniel Kearns

Commission Staff Advisory Opinion 15S-004
November 9, 2015

Page 4

Registration System. It appears that actual conflicts of interest will exist in deciding
regulations regarding licensure and annual renewal requirements for STRs (assuming
the city council members’ properties fall within the definition of properties affected). As
owners of properties/businesses prospectively subject to licensure, the city councilors
would be financially impacted by a mandate that all such properties pay a fee in order to
operate. Any city councilor with an actual conflict must publicly announce the conflict and
also refrain from participation in the matter [see ORS 244.120(2)].

Operational Requlations. |It appears that either actual or potential conflicts of interest will
arise on determining adoption of specific regulations for the purpose of establishing
standards of health and safety in the operation of STRs. However, the information
provided represents only generalizations of anticipated regulatory proposals in a way that
is too general to definitively determine each one as creating either an actual or potential
conflict of interest.

Again, assuming the city councilors’ properties meet the definition of properties subject
to a given operational regulation up for adoption by City Council, it appears, in general,
that actual conflicts of interest are most likely to occur. Any given operational regulation
is likely to have a financial impact on all subjected properties, especially regulations that
limit the use of properties (occupancy loads, parking requirements) or establish upkeep
requirements (trash collections, homeowner insurance review, safety inspections). On
the other hand, even if a city councilor’s property were to be subject to a regulation, if a
financial impact is nonetheless uncertain, contemplation of the given regulation may only
rise to a potential conflict.

Limiton Numbers. As to the question of adopting specific regulations for the purpose of
liming, or capping, the number of STRs in operation citywide, it appears that the city
councilors may experience either actual or potential conflicts of interest. However,
determining whether the conflict is actual or potential for either city councilor will depend
on whether that city councilor’s property would be or could be directly affected by the
individual regulation in contemplation. If City Council is deciding whether to approve a
regulation that would exclude a city councilor’s property from STR operation, or deciding
which to approve among a number of regulations, at least one of which would affect
operation of a city councilor’s STR, then an actual conflict of interest would appear to
exist for that city councilor.

Furthermore, even proposed regulations that would not necessarily appear to result in
financial impact (or exclusion) of a city councilors STR operation should nonetheless be
considered potential conflicts of interest. As a result of any sort of regulation effectively
limiting the number of operative STRs in the City, it is likely that some STRs, or STRs in
some areas, could experience an increase in rental business as a result of decreased or
limited competition although it is impossible to say with certainty.

QUESTION 2: Whether, in the event that any conflicts of interest exist, the city councilors
would be affected to the same degree as a larger class of persons per ORS
244.020(12)(b) so as to provide exemption from the announce and refrain requirements
for handling conflicts of interest under ORS 244.120.

ANSWER_ 2: ORS 244.020(12)(b) could apply to certain actions, decisions, or
recommendations by City Council that would affect, to the same degree, an identifiable
class within the City of Hood River.

ORS 244.020(12)(b) provides an exception to compliance with the conflict of interest
provisions under ORS 244.120 where official action, decision, or recommendation would
financially impact the conflicted public official, a relative, or any business with which either
is associated, to the same degree as a broader class of persons. If the conflicted city
councilors are determined to belong to such an identifiable group, and every member of
the group would be affected by City Council action to the same degree, then the “class
exception” may apply. The councilors would not be met with conflicts and would be
exempt from the disclosure and recusal requirements under ORS 244.120.

The Government Ethics Commission has the authority to determine whether a group
constitutes such a class. However, as mentioned above with regard to whether some of
the contemplated regulations would constitute actual or potential conflicts, the information
available as to each specific regulation is also too general and limited at this juncture to
make such a determination as to application of the “class exception.”

As City Council is currently in the process of determining which properties will be subject
to regulation as STRs, an OGEC determination as to whether the city councilors fall within
such a (not yet) defined group so as to constitute a class would appear to be premature.
Furthermore, even to the extent that any class exception may apply, the class might also
change depending on the particular regulation in question at a given time. Application of
the class exception can only be definitively determined in highly fact-specific
circumstances, such as on review of the individual, actual (or hypothetical or proposed)
regulation, where financial impact can be analyzed with specificity.

THIS RESPONSE ADDRESSES ONLY THE APPLICATION OF ORS 244 TO THE
FACTS STATED HEREIN. ANY RELEVANT INFORMATION, WHICH WAS NOT
INCLUDED BY THE REQUESTER OF THIS OPINION IN THE STATED FACTS,
COULD COMPLETELY CHANGE THE OUTCOME OF THIS OPINION. OTHER LAWS
OR REQUIREMENTS MAY ALSO APPLY. THIS IS NOT A FORMAL ADVISORY
OPINION PURSUANT TO ORS CHAPTER 244.280. THIS OPINION DOES NOT
EXEMPT A PUBLIC OFFICIAL FROM LIABILITY UNDER ORS CHAPTER 244 FOR
ANY ACTION OR TRANSACTION CARRIED OUT IN ACCORDANCE WITH THIS
OPINION. THIS OPINION IS ONLY MY PERSONAL ASSESSMENT AS THE
EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR OF THE OREGON GOVERNMENT ETHICS COMMISSION.

Daniel Kearns

Commission Staff Advisory Opinion 15S-004
November 9, 2015

Page 6

ADDENDUM

RELEVANT STATUTES: The following Oregon Revised Statutes (ORS) are applicable
to the issues that are addressed in this opinion:

ORS 244.020(1) “Actual conflict of interest” means any action or any decision or
recommendation by a person acting in a capacity as a public official, the effect of which
would be to the private pecuniary benefit or detriment of the person or the person’s
relative or any business with which the person or a relative of the person is associated
unless the pecuniary benefit or detriment arises out of circumstances described in
subsection (12) of this section.

ORS 244.020(12) “Potential conflict of interest” means any action or any decision or
recommendation by a person acting in a capacity as a public official, the effect of which
could be to the private pecuniary benefit or detriment of the person or the person’s
relative, or a business with which the person or the person’s relative is associated, unless
the pecuniary benefit or detriment arises out of the following:
(a) An interest or membership in a particular business, industry, occupation or
other class required by law as a prerequisite to the holding by the person of the
office or position.

(b) Any action in the person’s official capacity which would affect to the same
degree a class consisting of all inhabitants of the state, or a smaller class
consisting of an industry, occupation or other group including one of which or in
which the person, or the person’s relative or business with which the person or the
person’s relative is associated, is a member or is engaged.

(c) Membership in or membership on the board of directors of a nonprofit
corporation that is tax-exempt under section 501(c) of the Internal Revenue Code.

ORS 244.020(15) “Relative” means:

(a) The spouse, parent, stepparent, child, sibling, stepsibling, son-in-law or
daughter-in-law of the public official or candidate;

(b) The parent, stepparent, child, sibling, stepsibling, son-in-law or daughter-in-law
of the spouse of the public official or candidate;

(c) Any individual for whom the public official or candidate has a legal support
obligation;

(d) Any individual for whom the public official provides benefits arising from the
public official's public employment or from whom the public official receives
benefits arising from that individual’s employment; or

(e) Any individual from whom the candidate receives benefits arising from that

individual’s employment.

ORS 244.020(14) “Public official” means any person who, when an alleged violation of
this chapter occurs, is serving the State of Oregon or any of its political subdivisions or
any other public body as defined in ORS 174.109 as an elected official, appointed official,
employee or agent, irrespective of whether the person is compensated for the services.

ORS 244.120(2) An elected public official, other than a member of the Legislative
Assembly, or an appointed public official serving on a board or commission, shall:

(a) When met with a potential conflict of interest, announce publicly the nature of
the potential conflict prior to taking any action thereon in the capacity of a public
official; or

(b) When met with an actual conflict of interest, announce publicly the nature of
the actual conflict and:

(A) Except as provided in subparagraph (B) of this paragraph, refrain from
participating as a public official in any discussion or debate on the issue out
of which the actual conflict arises or from voting on the issue.

(B) If any public official’s vote is necessary to meet a requirement of a
minimum number of votes to take official action, be eligible to vote, but not
to participate as a public official in any discussion or debate on the issue
out of which the actual conflict arises.

ORS 244.130(1) When a public official gives notice of an actual or potential conflict of
interest, the public body as defined in ORS 174.109 that the public official serves shall
record the actual or potential conflict in the official records of the public body. In addition,
a notice of the actual or potential conflict and how it was disposed of may in the discretion
of the public body be provided to the Oregon Government Ethics Commission within a
reasonable period of time.
topics: Conflicts regarding a public official or business which a public official or a relative is associated
